title: YouTube as a source of patient information on erythema nodosum: an analysis of quality and reliability
screen_reason: QUALITY-ONLY study (excluded per section 1/section 3). The 61 English-language YouTube videos on erythema nodosum were scored only with generic instruments - Global Quality Scale, modified DISCERN, JAMA Benchmark Criteria and PEMAT-A/V. No item was ever judged true or false against an external ground truth: there is no fact-check, no guideline concordance coding, no 'accurate/inaccurate' or 'false/misleading' classification, and the word misinformation appears only in the aspiration to 'reduce misinformation'. The single share-type result (47.5% low quality, GQS 1-2) rests on a definition that mixes falsity with completeness - 'significant errors, inconsistencies, or major information gaps' - so a wholly accurate but shallow video receives the label, which section 3 assigns to QUALITY rather than CONTENT. No RECALL, EXPOSURE, REACH, SHARING or CONCENTRATION measure is reported either.
missed_or_uncertain: Values an adjudicator may want if the review decides to keep quality-only appendix rows after all (none were written, because the paper-level screen is EXCLUDE and section 5 requires an empty estimates list): GQS categories of the 61 videos - low quality (GQS 1-2) 29 (47.5%), moderate (GQS 3) 15 (24.6%), high (GQS 4-5) 17 (27.9%); by uploader, 40.7% of physician-uploaded videos were high quality vs 22.2% of those from independent/unspecified uploaders (Table 2 gives physician 7 (25.9%) low / 9 (33.3%) moderate / 11 (40.7%) high, n=27). Sample descriptors: 400 videos screened (first 100 for each of four search terms), 339 excluded, 61 analysed; uploader mix physician 27 (44.3%), patient 7 (11.4%), unspecified 27 (44.3%); format narrator only 23 (37.7%), patient experience 7 (11.5%), animation 7 (11.5%), slides 24 (39.3%). None of these is a falsity share. The paper reports no numerical count of erroneous claims, no per-claim accuracy audit and no engagement-weighted (exposure) share, so nothing here can be recovered as a prevalence estimate.

rob.design: Descriptive cross-sectional analysis. Single-day YouTube search (15 November 2025, 10:00-14:00 GMT+3) from a Turkey-based IP in incognito mode with cookies and history cleared, no account login, browser language English, default relevance ranking, four keywords ('erythema nodosum', '... causes', '... symptoms', '... treatment'), first 100 results each (400 screened). Exclusions: non-English, duplicates (by video ID and by title/duration/visual similarity), irrelevant, under 1 min or over 60 min, or defective audio/video; 61 videos analysed. Two researchers scored independently, disagreements first discussed then adjudicated by a third senior researcher; Cohen's kappa for GQS categorisation 0.72 (substantial), initial consensus on 53/61 videos (86.9%), 8 discordant (13.1%). Instruments: GQS (5-point), modified DISCERN (5 binary items), JAMA Benchmark Criteria (4 items), PEMAT-A/V. Kruskal-Wallis, Spearman rho, SPSS 29. Key limitation for this review: no veracity standard at all - quality and reliability are proxied by presentation and sourcing criteria, and uploader identity is self-declared (the authors note uploaders may not accurately disclose credentials). Popularity-truncated sample (first 100 per term) and a single search day.
rob.item6_quote: Low quality (score 1-2): Videos at this level contain significant errors, inconsistencies, or major information gaps that reduce their usability for instructional purposes. Moderate quality (score 3): While these videos possess a certain degree of educational value, they may lack depth, clarity, or comprehensive coverage. High quality (score 4-5): Videos in this category have accurate content, meticulous organization, and instructional value; therefore, they are considered to be effective and reliable educational material.
rob.item10_quote: Of the total videos, 47.5% (n = 29) were evaluated as low quality, 24.6% (n = 15) as moderate quality, and 27.9% (n = 17) as high quality.
